absaetze.t: Seit Oktober gibt es den "Tankrabatt". Verkehrsminister Bilger findet das richtig. Entlastung sei nötig gewesen, sagte er in der ARD-Arena. Kritisch blickt er auf Debatten über ein generelles Tempolimit.

Die Infrastruktur der Bahn ist marode, viele Straßen und Brücken müssen saniert werden und die Lage in Nahost trieb zuletzt die Spritpreise in die Höhe - die Herausforderungen des Bundesverkehrsministers Steffen Bilger sind groß. Seit Ende Juli ist er am Amt. In der ARD-Arena stellte er sich den Fragen von Bürgerinnen und Bürgern.

In dem TV-Format verteidigte er den "Tankrabatt". Viele Menschen, vor allem auf dem Land, seien auf das Auto angewiesen, sagte der CDU-Politiker. Die Preise an den Tankstellen seien seit vielen Monaten hoch. "Da war aus meiner Sicht einfach auch noch mal eine Entlastung nötig", sagte er.

Seit Anfang Oktober und noch bis Jahresende kassiert der Staat knapp 17 Cent weniger Steuern auf den Liter Sprit. Einen "Tankrabatt" gab es infolge des Iran-Konflikts mit Preissprüngen bereits im Frühjahr.
Bilger nennt Deutschlandticket weiterhin attraktiv

Umweltverbände hatten den erneuten Tankrabatt kritisiert - zumal auf der anderen Seite das Deutschlandticket im Nah- und Regionalverkehr 2027 teurer wird. Bilger nannte das Deutschlandticket auch bei der Preissteigerung im kommenden Jahr immer noch ein sehr attraktives Angebot.

Das Deutschlandticket kostet statt 63 Euro wie bisher ab Januar 66,80 Euro. Der Abo-Preis für 2027 wurde erstmals mit Hilfe einer bestimmten Formel berechnet. Ein Preisindex bildet auf Basis statistischer Daten die Kostenentwicklung etwa von Personal und Energie nach, die die Verkehrsunternehmen schultern müssen.

Weil das Ticket günstiger ist als bisherige regionale Abos, kommt es zu Einnahmeausfällen bei Verkehrsunternehmen. Deswegen geben Bund und Länder pro Jahr jeweils 1,5 Milliarden Euro - auch darauf verwies Bilger.
Minister spricht sich gegen generelles Tempolimit aus

Angesichts der hohen Spritpreise flammte die Diskussion über ein generelles Tempolimit zuletzt neu auf. In der ARD-Arena machte Bilger nun deutlich, dass er ein generelles Tempolimit auf deutschen Autobahnen ablehnt.

Es gebe, wenn man mal alle Straßen in ganz Deutschland anschaue, noch 4 Prozent Straßen, wo es kein Tempolimit gebe. Auf den Autobahnen seien es etwa 70 Prozent, wo es kein Tempolimit gibt. "Aber viele fahren jetzt ja auch schon langsamer, nutzen den Tempomat, wollen vielleicht auch Sprit sparen." Deswegen werde der CO2-Effekt überschätzt.
Es gebe gut ausgebaute Autobahnen in Deutschland. "Wir haben weniger Verkehrsunfälle als in anderen Ländern Europas, wo es ein Tempolimit gibt", sagte der Minister weiter.
Bilger sieht in Tempolimit "zusätzliche Spaltung"

Und: "Dann will ich schon auch um Verständnis werben, dass es für viele, die das Tempolimit ablehnen, schon auch eine Einschränkung ihrer Freiheit wäre, die, glaube ich, bei der vielen Spaltung, die wir in unserem Land haben, nochmal zusätzliche Spaltung verursachen würde."

Die Bundesregierung setze auf sogenannte Telematikanlagen, bei denen je nach Verkehrslage, nach Wetter und nach Stausituation die Geschwindigkeit angepasst werde. Die seien die intelligenteren Lösungen.

Die Grünen hatten in diesem Jahr erneut einen Vorstoß für die Einführung einer Höchstgeschwindigkeit von 130 Kilometern pro Stunde gemacht. Umweltverbände fordern seit Langem ein Tempolimit: Neben mehr Sicherheit könne ein Tempolimit auch zu deutlichen Einsparungen der klimaschädlichen CO2-Emissionen führen.
Die komplette Sendung der ARD-Arena finden Sie in der ARD-Mediathek.

items.titel: MQ-58 Valkyrie Drones Now Cost $6M-$8M Each
items.anriss: Kratos has provided an interesting update on the price of its Valkyrie drones . The uncrewed aircraft currently cost roughly $6 to $8 million, depending on their configuration and without certain mission systems installed. Though this is a …

absaetze.t: Kratos has provided an interesting update on the price of its Valkyrie drones. The uncrewed aircraft currently cost roughly $6 to $8 million, depending on their configuration and without certain mission systems installed. Though this is a more expensive price point than Kratos has said it has been aiming for in the past, it still puts Valkyrie firmly at the lower end of the cost spectrum for Collaborative Combat Aircraft (CCA) type drones based on available information, while still providing relatively high-end capabilities.

Kratos’ President and CEO Eric DeMarco shared the new cost figures, as well as other new details about the Valkyrie program, during a recent quarterly earnings call. He also spent considerable time talking about his view that affordability will be a central key factor for prospective customers for CCA-type drones going forward.

“I would not want to be anyone else than Kratos with the Valkyrie, that’s in production, that comes off the line, ‘white tail,’ six million dollars or something like that, maybe eight [million dollars], depending on configuration,” DeMarco said at one point during the call. “Missionized is more.”

Some more context is necessary before any more discussion of these cost figures. DeMarco’s remarks here were part of a lengthy response to a question about Kratos’ view of potential U.S. opportunities for sales of CCA-type drones in the next year.

The U.S. Air Force has been operating a small number of XQ-58As since the type first flew in 2019, in support of research and development and test and evaluation activities. The Marine Corps also experimented with the XQ-58A and is now in the process of acquiring a fully missionized version of the Valkyrie for operational use through that service’s CCA program. Those drones are sometimes referred to as the MQ-58Bs. Northrop Grumman is technically the prime contractor for the Marine effort, which falls under the umbrella of the larger Marine Air-Ground Task Force Uncrewed Expeditionary Tactical Aircraft (MUX TACAIR) program.

Kratos has also secured at least two other contracts for Valkyries from other still-unidentified customers. At least one of them is outside of the United States and took delivery of drones back in the third quarter of 2025. The company is known to be pursuing a bid to supply a version of the Valkyrie called the U740 to the German Air Force, or Luftwaffe, through a partnership with Airbus. The U740 made its first flight at an unnamed test facility in northern Europe last month.

At the time of writing, Valkyrie drones fall into two main categories, at least that we know of. These are rocket-assisted takeoff (RATO) versions, which lack landing gear, and landing gear-equipped conventional takeoff and landing (CTOL) types that operate from traditional runways. The U.S. Air Force’s XQ-58As, as well as the European U740, are RATO types. The MQ-58Bs the Marines are acquiring are CTOL versions.

Kratos has also developed a special launch trolley so RATO drones can take off from a runway. No matter how they get into the air, drones in the RATO configuration land via parachute at the end of a sortie. CTOL drones can also be launched via the RATO method, but then land on a traditional runway.

In March 2024, before the CTOL version was officially disclosed, Kratos told TWZ that there were at least five distinct subvariants of the Valkyrie. The company has been steadily working to expand the performance envelope of the core design since its first flight in 2019, too.

Going back to the matter of the Valkyrie’s unit price, DeMarco had put the figure at around $6.5 million back in 2023. The following year, he told TWZ directly that the price range for RATO versions, specifically, was between $4 and $6 million. At that time, he said the $4 million figure reflected economies of scale benefits from a production run of 100 drones. Kratos had said years ago now that it was hoping to eventually be able to drive down the price point to $2 million apiece as production ramped up. As of August, the company’s stated goal was to get to an annual production rate of 40 airframes by 2028.
As noted earlier, even at $8 million, Valkyrie’s unit cost is deeply at the lower end of the known spectrum for CCA-type designs.

General Atomics and Anduril are both on contract now to build batches of their respective FQ-42A Vengeance and FQ-44A Fury drone designs under the first phase of the U.S. Air Force’s CCA program, or Increment 1. The service has said that it is aiming to have at least 500 of those uncrewed aircraft in inventory by 2032. The Air Force also expects to acquire additional CCAs, which could be of entirely different designs, through a follow-on Increment 2. Kratos could potentially submit a bid for that competition.

The Air Force has said that it is targeting a $20 million average unit cost for Increment 1 CCAs once full-scale production is achieved, but what the actual price point will be remains to be seen. There has been talk previously of the price range of the designs we are seeing now being between $20 and $30 million. Anduril has said that each Fury will be cheaper than that, but has yet to provide a hard figure. At the time of writing, it is unclear whether General Atomics has yet shared any hard cost data of its own.

Boeing’s MQ-28 Ghost Bat, another CCA-type design originally developed for the Royal Australian Air Force and in limited production now, offers another point of comparison. In 2024, authorities in Australia said Boeing was aiming for the Ghost Bat’s unit cost to be “10 per cent of the cost of a crewed aircraft such as a[n F-35] Joint Strike Fighter.” At that time, this would have translated to between $8 and $10 million based on publicly available F-35 cost data. How that cost projection has evolved since then, and how it applies to the larger Block 3 version Boeing now has in development, is unknown.

“Affordability is gonna win,” Kratos CEO DeMarco said on the recent earnings call. “We build 150 to 200 jet drones every year. I think more than anyone else in the world, Kratos does [sic], target and tactical. And our bill of materials across the target drones and the tactical drones is substantially the same, which gives us leverage on the supply chain. No one can hit our price points, cost points. Can’t do it.”
“I believe we’re going to win ultimately globally, including in the U.S. because of capability and affordability,” he added.
DeMarco also highlighted last month’s first flight of the U740 variant as another reflection of potential foreign sales opportunities for the Valkyrie.

“We’re flying internationally. What does that mean? We had to get State Department approval,” he explained. “You don’t see anyone else flying internationally, do you? They talk about it. We’re going to fly here. We’re going to fly there. We’re going to build it here. We’re going to build it there. No one’s done it but us. That is a huge, ginormous competitive advantage for us with international customers because we can bring them airplanes and fly them for them on their ranges, and, heretofore, no one else can.”

All this being said, it is important to remember that, despite Kratos’ significant success with Valkyrie in recent years, the drone’s continued development has not been without hurdles. TWZ was the first to report on the crash of one of these drones in a still-unknown “test configuration” on August 4. That mishap occurred at the U.S. Army’s Dugway Proving Ground in Utah, a known hub for uncrewed aircraft testing.

“No one was injured in the incident. As safety is our top priority, flight test operations for this system have been paused temporarily in an abundance of caution while we investigate the cause of the incident,” Kratos told TWZ in a statement at the time. “Kratos has additional test systems ready once the investigation is complete.”

“We push the envelope across all of our system types,” Steve Fendley, President of Kratos’ Unmanned Systems Division, also subsequently told TWZ. “The other thing I can say is we are constantly increasing the capability of the system, both for what we think it needs to be, and in other cases to satisfy what a particular customer may want to do to satisfy a certain mission.”
The crash at Dugway did not come up at all during the recent earnings call, despite it having occurred during the quarter under discussion.

Furthermore, DeMarco’s comments underscore just how much the CCA market is heating up, and not just in the United States. There has been an explosion in the development of relevant designs in recent years globally. This extends to potential adversaries, too, especially China.
Kratos is clearly hoping that Valkyrie’s price point, together with other attributes of the still-evolving design, will help it continue to stand out in this still-growing field of major competitors.

items.titel: Security Levels At U.S. Bases In England Raised Without Explanation
items.anriss: At least two bases in England hosting U.S. Air Force aircraft are operating under beefed-up security protocols, a U.S. official told us Monday afternoon. The official was responding to our questions about what appeared to be unusual …

absaetze.t: At least two bases in England hosting U.S. Air Force aircraft are operating under beefed-up security protocols, a U.S. official told us Monday afternoon. The official was responding to our questions about what appeared to be unusual aircraft movements out of RAF Mildenhall. It is unclear what spurred these measures, how long they have been in place or whether they are connected to an ongoing investigation into whether Iran was behind a security incident at RAF Fairford in September that reportedly prompted the hasty departure of B-1 Lancer bombers.

“Enhanced force protection measures are in effect across RAF Lakenheath and RAF Mildenhall,” the official told us. “We constantly assess a variety of factors that determine what measures we institute or modify to protect our installations, our people and their families. We are working closely with our host nation counterparts to minimize impacts from enhanced force protection activities and ensure the safety of U.S. personnel, their families and the local community.”
The official declined to say what steps were taken.
“For operational security reasons, we do not discuss specific force protection measures,” the official added.

RAF Mildenhall and RAF Lakenheath are both major hubs for the U.S. Air Force. Mildenhall’s host unit is the 100th Air Refueling Wing, which operates KC-135 Stratotanker aerial refueling jets. The base is also home to Air Force RC-135V/W Rivet Joint reconnaissance aircraft, Air Force Special Operations Command (AFSOC) CV-22 Osprey tiltrotor aircraft and MC-130J Commando II special operations cargo planes. Lakenheath hosts Air Force F-15E Strike Eagle and F-35A Lightning II aircraft.
Both bases also see frequent flights transiting to other locations.

As we noted earlier in this piece, the official was responding to our questions about unusual aircraft movements out of Mildenhall. They were first noticed by the @DefenceGeek open-source flight tracker account.

“Over the course of today, a number of US Air Force assets at RAF Mildenhall (EGUN) have made unannounced/unexpected movements to other locations, with several of those movements in motion presently,” DefenceGeek wrote on X. “The initial few this morning I assumed were due to heavy fog in the area, but other information is now suggesting something else… – Several KC-135s have moved to Spangdahlem (ETAD) or Prestwick (EGPK) – CV-22Bs have moved from Mildenhall to Lakenheath It remains unclear if there is an ongoing exercise or information of a potential threat (following the incident at RAF Fairford)…”
DefenceGeek also noted that RAF Lakenheath posted a notice this morning on Facebook urging vigilance in spotting and reporting drones.

“Our strongest security asset is an observant community,” the RAF Lakenheath Facebook post read. “Staying vigilant and reporting suspicious activity, including unauthorized drone activity, helps protect our Airmen, families and mission. If you see something unusual on or around the Tri-Base area, report it to Security Forces.”

It is unclear what connection, if any, the Lakenheath post has to the enhanced force protection status. U.S. Air Forces in Europe – Air Forces Africa (USAFE) declined to discuss security measures. The command oversees U.S. Air Force operations in Europe and Africa.

“U.S. Air Force aircraft rotate between installations and operating locations for a variety of reasons including training and real world requirements,” USAFE told us. “U.S. military aircraft are hosted in accordance with access, basing, and overflight agreements with our Allies and partners. Due to operations security, we will not provide further information on movement of assets.”

The departures from Mildenhall took place amid an ongoing flow of refueling tankers and other aircraft to the Middle East as President Donald Trump continues to mull whether to resume strikes against Iran. This afternoon, Trump wrapped up his meeting with Qatari Prime Minister Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani to discuss a flagging effort to resolve the conflict with Iran through diplomacy.
It should also be noted that in late November 2024, Lakenheath, Mildenhall and two other RAF bases hosting U.S. forces experienced drone incursions, which we were the first to write about.
As we mentioned earlier in this piece, security concerns about bases in England hosting U.S. Air Force aircraft and personnel were raised following an incident at RAF Fairford.

Like Mildenhall and Lakenheath, RAF Fairford is a major hub for U.S. military aircraft in the United Kingdom. It is a regular host of strategic assets, including bombers and U-2 spy planes. It also acts as a pit stop for other aircraft, including fighters, that are being ferried to and from the United States. Bomber strikes launched from Fairford were a central aspect of major U.S. combat operations against Iran earlier this year.

In late September, five men were arrested on suspicion of driving bomb-laden vans toward it. They were soon released on bail after no explosives were found, but two men were later arrested, one of who was “charged with assisting a foreign intelligence service, which police earlier said they believed to be Iran,” according to the BBC.

A week after the security incident, U.S. Air Force B-1B Lancer bombers that had been deployed to RAF Fairford in the U.K. since Operation Epic Fury returned to their home stations, a U.S. defense official confirmed to TWZ at the time. The hasty movement was reportedly sparked by new Iranian threats against the base. As we previously reported, Tehran directly threatened RAF Fairford in July over its use as a base to launch attacks against Iran.

We can’t say for sure what prompted the enhanced security at RAF Lakenheath and RAF Mildenhall or whether the aircraft movements at Mildenhall are precautionary or just normal shifting of resources. We will continue to monitor the situation and provide updates when warranted.

items.titel: Democracy depends on more than simply banning a far-right news channel
items.anriss: On Saturday, in Trappes, a suburb west of Paris, hundreds of residents gathered to mourn Pengo Bossio Wangi, a 26-year-old man shot dead on 23 October. During the attack, a gunman opened fire from a car, killing Wangi and injuring seven …

absaetze.t: On Saturday, in Trappes, a suburb west of Paris, hundreds of residents gathered to mourn Pengo Bossio Wangi, a 26-year-old man shot dead on 23 October. During the attack, a gunman opened fire from a car, killing Wangi and injuring seven people, including a 12-year-old girl, in what police have called a terrorist act motivated by racism. Among the banners displayed at vigils was one that read “CNews Kills”. The broadcaster, which runs one of France’s most watched rolling-news channels, has consistently portrayed Trappes as an Islamist hotbed and the suspect in the shooting told investigators that he had chosen the area in order to target Muslim and African people. Speaking to investigative newspaper Mediapart, his friends described how he had become consumed by the racist rhetoric that he watched on television.

In the days following the Trappes killing, public outrage crystallised around a petition demanding that CNews be banned, which gathered more than a million signatures and triggered calls for a debate in the Assemblée Nationale. CNews features relentless punditry and misinformation, and normalises guests with racist views. Inspired by Rupert Murdoch’s Fox News, the channel has been transformed under the ownership of billionaire Vincent Bolloré – whose media empire includes Canal+ – as part of an avowed strategy to bring the far right to power. Despite its clear breaching of France’s anti-hate legislation, CNews is able to weather the storm of financial penalties thanks to its owner’s deep pockets. Arcom, the country’s media regulator, has so far issued fines totalling €630,000.

In 2024, Arcom revoked the broadcasting licence of C8, a major entertainment channel also owned by Bolloré, due to its promotion of misinformation and conspiracy theories. Experts, however, argue that banning CNews is not only constitutionally impossible but also that it would come too late. The channel’s rhetoric has permeated other rolling-news channels, including formerly trusted public broadcasters. A ban could also benefit Marine Le Pen by opening the door to an Viktor Orbán-style assault on media freedom were she to come to power in next year’s presidential elections.

Instead, regulators must bring stricter scrutiny to bear on media acquisitions by introducing safeguards against excessive ownership concentration and protecting outlets so that they can survive without billionaire owners. The public must be convinced that supporting independent journalism is an investment in the future of democracy. In an age of information warfare, media pluralism is a matter of national security. For those already bearing the consequences of a failure to act, the stakes could not be higher. As night fell on Saturday, Trappes mayor Ali Rabeh addressed the crowd. “To the free press of this country: refuse them the right to call themselves peers of your wonderful calling and to let far-right activists hide behind a press card. Realise that you are their next target. Open your eyes, before it is too late.”
Antoine Gouillon is a Paris-based journalist. For more opinion, analysis and insight,subscribeto Monocle today.

items.titel: Mona Chalabi Paints a Picture of Class Inequality
items.anriss: “As an adult and as a journalist, I have stared shamelessly.” That refusal to look away is precisely what data journalist, writer, and artist Mona Chalabi has built her deeply principled career on. Known best for her indelible data …

absaetze.t: “The crisis is the system that we’re in,” the Pulitzer Prize-winning data journalist and artist says in an interview with Hyperallegic about her first book, “Ten Lives.”
November 9, 2026 — 13 min read

“As an adult and as a journalist, I have stared shamelessly.” That refusal to look away is precisely what data journalist, writer, and artist Mona Chalabi has built her deeply principled career on. Known best for her indelible data visualizations, from the obscenity of Jeff Bezos’s wealth to the Israeli government’s starvation of Palestinians in Gaza and the racial and gender biases in museum collections, the Pulitzer Prize-winning Iraqi-British journalist tackles the subject of wealth and economic inequality in America in her first book, Ten Lives: How What We Have Shapes Who We Are (2026).

When I met her in the West Village in September, she’d just come from recording its accompanying audiobook, a delicate process given the visuals on its pages. Chalabi organized meticulous interviews conducted with anonymous subjects across income levels over the course of six years into 10 vividly fleshed-out characters. Each represents a particular economic class, illustrated in her signature hand-drawn style and punctuated by reflections on her own financial struggles as a young journalist and, more recently, in the wake of her mother’s illness. Chalabi carries a long tradition of data visualization — W.E.B. Du Bois’s The Exhibit of American Negroes comes to mind — into her refreshing candor about class and the stifling silence around it, particularly in journalism and the art world.

That insistence on specificity and honesty in her reporting goes hand-in-hand with her political advocacy; Chalabi donated her $15,000 Pulitzer Prize award to the Palestinian Journalists Syndicate and has been fighting for Palestinian rights since she was a teenager. Her drive to seek out and represent truth, in Ten Lives and in her social media posts, is anchored in a sensitivity and profound sense of responsibility. In this way, she restores some of the humanity and dignity to the statistics that capture the brutality of genocide, exploitation, and economic inequality, one brushstroke at a time. In an interview, we spoke about the financial realities of journalism, the value of collaboration in an era of isolation, and the art and literature that sustains her. Our conversation has been lightly edited for clarity and length.

Hyperallergic: In the intro to Ten Lives, you recall getting scolded for not observing “the etiquette of looking away” as a child. And it’s so striking that you have made a career of doing the opposite. How did you decide to make class, something we’re taught to overlook from a young age, the subject of this book?
Mona Chalabi: The first line of the original manuscript said, “I wrote this book because I was paid a shitload of money to write it.”
H: Ha!

MC: And my editor was like, “Yeah, you can't do that. No one's gonna want to read a book that you wrote simply for money.” But I also knew that this was a commercial idea, and that did inform it. I have been quite shameless about the fact that I want my work to reach a wide audience. That has always, always mattered to me. It was the beginning of the pandemic, and part of the way that I pitched it was this idea that there's gonna be a big financial crisis and the dynamics are more nuanced than simply talking about the one percent. There's this idea of a coming economic collapse or a coming financial crisis. But as soon as we're in it, it's not this cyclical model. The crisis is the system that we're in that is so broken.

H: That gradation of class that usually doesn't get talked about is such a crucial contribution of this book. What led you to stratify these stories based on subcategories that often just get collapsed into “working class, middle class, upper class”?

MC: Class is really informative about who I am and how I move through the world and my relationships. And I felt like it was really, really lacking in our discourse. I feel a bit hesitant to use the word “discourse,” but it's just true. And it's not just about discourse, it's more mundane than that. It's the way that someone like me can say, “I'm an Arab, cis, heterosexual woman,” with total ease, but class doesn't really come into it. There's a dishonesty there. Actually, class is really, really important. And many of us aren't really talking about that in accurate and fruitful ways.

items.titel: Canada’s proposed federal budget includes tax breaks for artists and $554m funding boost for museums
items.anriss: Like the Liberal government’s 2025 budget proposal, this year’s also calls for adopting an artist’s resale right policy

absaetze.t: The proposed budget Canada’s Liberal government released on 5 November offers the country’s artists a lifeline, recommending new tax measures and funding channels. In a post on X, shortly after finance minister François-Philippe Champagne tabled the budget, the Prime Minister Mark Carney wrote that “if you’re a Canadian artist, you won’t pay tax on up to $45,000” ($31,800) of income from their creative work.

Much remains unknown about how this tax exemption and other measures would be implemented. The budget released last week only proposes a tax credit and the federal government has yet to set its cost, start date or eligibility rules. Ottawa says its planned consultations with Canadians and the cultural sector will be announced in the spring 2027 economic update.

The proposed budget also includes C$783.1m ($554m) over five years going toward the National Arts Centre, Library and Archives Canada, the National Battlefields Commission and national museums, according to The Canadian Press. It also promises free entry to national museums for visitors under age 25, funded through a subsidy of C$46.3m ($32.8m) over five years, then C$11.5m ($8.1m) per year. The budget also calls for increasing funding to the Canada Council for the Arts with a new investment of C$20m ($14.1m) over three years.

“This funding falls far short of what is actually needed: permanent, stable funding at a scale that enables impactful support for Canadian artists and institutions,” Jenna Faye Powell, the interim national executive director of Carfac (Canadian Artists’ Representation/Le Front des Artistes Canadiens), tells The Art Newspaper.

In addition to funding boosts and tax breaks for artists, the budget reiterates support for the long-promised adoption of artist’s resale rights in Canada, which would provide artists with royalties from secondary-market sales of their work. In the 2025 Budget, the government announced its intent to amend the Copyright Act to create an artist’s resale right in Canada, but the legislation never materialised.

Adopting an artist’s resale right “would provide creators of original visual artworks with a royalty each time their work is resold through an eligible sale, creating an additional source of income”, Carfac and the Regroupement des Artistes en Arts Visuels (RAAV) wrote in a joint statement. More than 100 countries around the world have artist’s resale right laws on the books, although neither Canada nor the United States has adopted such a policy despite multiple attempts.

“As a sector, we still have a lot of questions, while many artists need relief now,” Powell says. “Especially those still grappling with tariffs. Carfac will certainly push to be a part of that consultation process.”

For the Vancouver-based artist and pioneer of photo-conceptualism Ian Wallace, the proposed budget’s measures for supporting artists and the arts sector are welcome news. “Generous support of Canadian museums allowing them to build their collections by purchasing the work of emerging artists” is an important part of development of contemporary Canadian art history, he says, as is academic research and discourse around contemporary Canadian art.

Wallace adds that the tax credit is a “generous one”, although he says that “most Canadian artists are not selling more than C$45,000 a year in any case” and their yearly taxable income fluctuates wildly.

“When Canadian artists are doing their, work it’s not just to get by and pay the rent,” Wallace says. “It’s to contribute something to the overall culture. That’s the value of it: to show that there is a valuable cultural history in Canada that we are proud of and can articulate.” He adds: “I’m happy to see that artists and what they’re doing is respected and supported in the federal budget.”

As for the artist’s resale right legislation, Wallace has a more nuanced outlook. The law would apply to secondary-market sales that occur “outside of the normal sale structure that happens through a gallery that represents the artist”, he says. “In that sense, suddenly there’s another legal structure to deal with that might or might not be work well. I’m obviously for anything that supports the artist, but I can see some more bureaucratic and financial complications coming up with the artist’s resale right.” But, he adds, that is “more of a problem for collectors and institutions than artists”.

items.titel: Clouds Were Once Photography’s Greatest Challenge
items.anriss: The original 1996 Windows XP default background is arguably the most viewed photo of all time; its cumulus puffs drifting across a way-too-blue sky are seared into my and countless others’ Y2K childhoods. Such images of fluffy clouds are …

absaetze.t: The Met Museum’s “Chasing Clouds” is a pleasing romp through the technical problem of capturing clouds at photography’s beginning.
November 9, 2026 — 2 min read

The original 1996 Windows XP default background is arguably the most viewed photo of all time; its cumulus puffs drifting across a way-too-blue sky are seared into my and countless others’ Y2K childhoods. Such images of fluffy clouds are so ubiquitous that it’s hard to believe they once presented one of photography’s greatest technological challenges. The Met exhibition Chasing Clouds is a pleasing romp through the history of this problem through a union of art and science, spanning the early 1800s to 1929 — roughly photography’s first century. While the medium showed promise as “the pencil of nature,” its first processes were overly sensitive to blue light, registering the sky as a blank white space, impossibly overexposed.

While this lent some images a minimalist mystique, like John Beasley Greene’s “The Nile in Front of the Theban Hills” (1853–54), other photographers resorted to painting clouds into their landscapes by hand. An initial breakthrough came when French photographer Gustave Le Gray figured out how to stitch together two pictures — one calibrated to sky, and the other to land and sea. (Photographic fakery is as old as the medium itself.)

Though the exhibition begins with painted cloud studies and ends with photographic modernism, visual discoveries unfold in a dialogue between painting and technology rather than as a scientific march from one to the other. This makes for a much more interesting story; obsolescence is often a capitalist public relations trick.
